additional_context:
[Council feedback on the previous definition]
From model_reviewer:
- proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.primary_joint_actions: The hugging and pulling-in action of the arms is not represented. The frames show elbows flexed, the stone clasped against the abdomen and chest, and the arms squeezing it. The instructions say to pull the stone into the torso and then get it high onto the chest. The assumption that arm work can be modeled only through stabilization demands is unsupported. The chosen demands (elbow_stability, shoulder_position_hold, grip, wrist_stability) do not reach the elbow flexors or the adductors and extensors of the shoulder. As a result brachialis, long and short heads of biceps brachii, latissimus dorsi, teres major and the sternocostal pectoralis major are zero or near zero, although they are clearly loaded when a heavy stone is hugged and lifted. Suggested correction: Add the arm actions that hold and pull the stone in, with emphasis set to assist if they are not the main movers. Elbow_joint/flexion would cover brachialis and biceps. Glenohumeral_joint/adduction and/or horizontal_adduction would cover latissimus dorsi, teres major and pectoralis major. Glenohumeral_joint/extension could cover the pull into the torso. Use sides both for these bilateral actions.
[End of council feedback]

assumptions: The concentric phase is modeled as the lift from the floor, through the lap, to the loading platform.
Hip extension and knee extension are the primary movers, as in a deadlift-to-squat-to-stand lift.

The arms hug and pull the stone into the torso. Elbow flexion, shoulder adduction and shoulder extension are credited as assist actions on both arms, because they hold and draw in the load rather than move it through the main range.
Ankle plantarflexion is an assist action, as in squats and cleans.
The trunk is braced and held against flexion under load, so the spinal erectors are credited through anti_flexion_spine and intra_abdominal_pressure rather than a lumbar extension action.
Grip is credited because the fingers are placed under and around the stone.
The final lean-back phase is treated as the hip extension that finishes the lift, not as a separate spinal extension.
The variant is the standard stone-to-platform lift with a lap, performed for repetitions.
classification_reasons: The exercise is a bilateral, two-footed lift in which the stone is hugged, pulled off the floor, lapped and driven up to a platform. Hip and knee extension do the lifting, and the arms hold the stone close.
The supplied joint-action, stabilization and movement-family vocabulary can represent the whole lift faithfully.

The contact sheet shows a bilateral hip-hinged setup with the stone between the feet, then a deep squat position with the stone hugged against the abdomen and chest. This agrees with the instructions.

instructions: Begin with the atlas stone between your feet. Bend at the hips to wrap your arms vertically around the Atlas Stone, attempting to get your fingers underneath the stone. Many stones will have a small flat portion on the bottom, which will make the stone easier to hold.
Pulling the stone into your torso, drive through the back half of your feet to pull the stone from the ground.
As the stone passes the knees, lap it by sitting backward, pulling the stone on top of your thighs.

Sit low, getting the stone high onto your chest as you change your grip to reach over the stone. Stand, driving through with your hips. Close distance to the loading platform, and lean back, extending the hips to get the stone as high as possible.
